name: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
answer: An AI enablement audit in finance examines how an organization prepares, deploys, and oversees AI systems across financial operations, from credit decisioning and fraud detection to reporting and customer service. It covers the inventory of models and tools, the data they use, the people accountable for them, and the controls around access, change, and output. The audit also looks at whether AI use aligns with internal policies and external regulatory expectations for safety, fairness, and record keeping. It is not a technical code review but a structured check of enablement: whether the business can show what is running, why, and with what oversight.

sections.body: An AI enablement audit in finance examines how an organization prepares, deploys, and oversees AI systems across financial operations, from credit decisioning and fraud detection to reporting and customer service. It covers the inventory of models and tools, the data they use, the people accountable for them, and the controls around access, change, and output. The audit also looks at whether AI use aligns with internal policies and external regulatory expectations for safety, fairness, and record keeping. It is not a technical code review but a structured check of enablement: whether the business can show what is running, why, and with what oversight.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit reviews the infrastructure that supports AI in finance, including data platforms, model registries, deployment pipelines, and monitoring systems. It checks where models are hosted, whether on internal servers, cloud services, or third-party vendor systems, and how data flows into and out of them. Attention goes to access controls, encryption, logging, and the ability to reproduce a model's inputs and outputs for audit evidence. The infrastructure section also considers whether the organization can isolate or shut down a model quickly if it behaves unexpectedly.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Auditors typically map the AI lifecycle from business need and data sourcing through development, validation, deployment, and retirement. They interview model owners, review documentation such as model cards and risk assessments, and test a sample of decisions or outputs against expected behavior. The work often includes checking for data leakage, drift, and unauthorized changes between development and production. Because many finance teams use vendor or embedded AI, the method also covers due diligence on third-party tools and the contracts that define responsibility.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: This section focuses on accountability, policies, and evidence. The audit checks whether there is a named owner for each AI system, a defined approval process before deployment, and regular review after launch. It examines how the organization handles bias, explainability, privacy, and incident response, and whether records are kept in a way that satisfies auditors and regulators. Rights and risk are treated as operational questions: who can change a model, who can see its outputs, and what happens when a customer or counterparty disputes an automated decision. Provenance matters because finance requires a clear chain from data source to final output.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The AI enablement audit is moving from a one-off project to a continuous control function, with more automated evidence collection and real-time monitoring of model behavior. Regulators are paying closer attention to AI in credit, insurance, trading, and anti-money laundering, so audit scope is expanding to include generative AI tools used by staff and embedded in vendor software. Future audits will likely require standardized model inventories, machine-readable documentation, and stronger testing for adversarial or unexpected inputs. The direction is toward treating AI systems like financial reporting systems: subject to the same rigor of internal control, external assurance, and traceable change management.
